text: Ninety-three minutes is not long to take over a city, and the film spends none of them explaining itself. Tony Camonte comes up in the Chicago of the 1920s as somebody else's muscle, and what follows is a record of how fast a man stops taking orders: territory, supply, the removal of whoever stands one rung above him. Howard Hawks runs it at the tempo of a business story with the manners of a comedy, so the laugh and the gunfire keep landing in the same minute. What throws the machine off is private. Camonte watches his sister with an attention that answers to nothing in the ledger, and the picture keeps returning to it as though that were the real account. Made in 1932, near enough to the headlines to play less like a moral about crime than a study of appetite that has found a market.

The freight goes out in any weather or the contract goes to somebody else, and in a remote South American port that arithmetic is settled on whoever is next in the rotation. Howard Hawks hands the ledger to the man who runs the airline and lets him keep his face still while he does the sums on his own pilots. A traveling performer comes off a boat into the middle of it, which is how the outsider's questions get asked out loud. Most of the two hours happen on the ground, in a room of men waiting for the sky to clear; the Academy's award went to the special effects, that is, to the flying, which is the smaller half of the drama. Romance in here has to fit around a schedule indifferent to it, and the people conducting it are careful about what they ask for.

A boat, two women, one man, a horizon with nothing on it: everything the situation contains is visible in the first minutes, and nearly two hours remain. What fills them is not rescue but recollection, each life opened in turn while the water keeps its own time underneath. Mário Peixoto made it in Brazil in 1931 with no house style to answer to, and it takes the liberties that follow: shots running well past the point where information stops, an eye left to work on drift, texture, the difference between one grey and another. Abraccine's ranking of the hundred best Brazilian films holds a place for it, which is a strange fate for a picture that never quite consents to tell a story. Confinement is the subject, and it is built almost entirely out of open space.

The factory has closed, a payment has been promised, and the village has nothing to do but wait for it. Béla Tarr gives that wait seven hours and twelve minutes, which is not an endurance test but an argument: a place emptying out cannot be described at the speed of a plot. Everyone's business is everyone's here, among a doctor and three couples and the drink and the weather and the arithmetic of who can leave, and the film moves at walking pace because that is the pace at which the place is lived. Then a man the others believed dead comes back with a proposal, and the attention shifts from erosion to persuasion. Communism has fallen somewhere above them. At ground level the pressure is the roof, the money, the neighbour's opinion, and how little it takes for people with nothing to hand it over.

Harold Bissonette would like it known that the name is pronounced bis-on-ay. Sixty-eight minutes is all the time needed to charge him for that dignity, repeatedly: an inheritance, a grocery counter he is glad to be rid of, a California orange grove bought unseen and reported worthless, and a wife who objects to every part of the plan at a volume he cannot get out of. The method is obstruction. Every simple intention, to sell, to pack, to sleep, meets a person or an object with other business, and the gag is held one beat past where it should have finished, then a beat after that. Nothing in the plot moves much. What carries it is a man's refusal to concede that the day has been ruined, and the patience with which the world keeps proving that it has.

The assassination has already happened when the film begins; what is left is a week that has to be got through in public. Pablo Larraín stays inside those days with Jacqueline Kennedy, at the distance a camera keeps from a person who knows she is being looked at. Grief here is partly an administrative matter. There are arrangements to make, rooms to hand over, wording to settle, and every decision will be photographed and kept. The film is less curious about what she felt than about the gap between the face she offers and the one she does not, and it holds both in a single shot without ruling on which is true. A hundred minutes, all of them after the fact. It is a small film about an enormous event, and the smallness is the argument.

Some of what this documentary presents as found was arranged in front of the camera. Luis Buñuel went to Las Hurdes, in the province of Cáceres, in 1932, and came back with thirty minutes pitched in the register of a geography lesson: a region introduced, its resources counted, its people observed. The staging is the pressure the film applies. Anyone who trusts the format is asked to notice what the format permits — that hunger can be narrated in an even tone, that the young leaving for work elsewhere can be filed as a demographic fact, that a camera can stand in a village and alter nothing. Made in Spain in 1933, it sits on neither side of the line between reportage and fiction, and half an hour is long enough for that to become uncomfortable.

Twenty-five thousand dollars, and then the father will consent to the wedding. That errand gets postponed for most of the film, which is the point: Lucky misses his own ceremony, turns up in New York with a business partner and no money, meets a dance instructor named Penny, and thereafter the negotiating is done in the numbers rather than the dialogue. Two people who cannot say anything directly say all of it by matching each other's footwork. George Stevens keeps the comedy quick and the songs unhurried, and leaves two earlier attachments hanging over the arrangement so that every step forward is charged for with a step back. The plot is a pretext and knows it. What is settled on the floor is whether these two agree about anything.

The assignment is a disappearance nobody solved and a family archive nobody outside the family has read. Mikael Blomkvist takes it because he has just lost a libel case to the industrialist he tried to expose, and a publisher with a ruined name suddenly has time on his hands. The other half of the film belongs to a young hacker who works nothing like he does and has never had cause to expect an institution to help her. Niels Arden Oplev spends 152 minutes at the pace of an archive rather than a chase: papers, photographs, interviews, long drives to reach relatives who would rather not talk. It took the Guldbagge for best film, and what holds up is less the puzzle than the plainness with which the crimes underneath it are handled.

A Bronx parish school, 1964: a nun decides something is wrong, and the film never produces the evidence that would settle it. Two women watch the same new priest and arrive at different temperatures about him. The boy at the centre of it is the school's African-American student, and that bears on every judgment made anywhere in the building. John Patrick Shanley keeps the scale at the size of the argument — an office, a classroom, the corridor between them — so the pressure has to come from vocabulary and tone: who may ask a question, who may end a conversation, what a shift in a voice is permitted to prove. Certainty is the thing under examination, and the film is exact about what it costs the person holding it.

Mike Lazaridis wants the thing to work; Jim Balsillie wants the meeting. The company they build between them made the first smartphone, and that is the least interesting fact in the film, whose actual subject is the engineering room and what arrives in it once money starts coming on a schedule. Matt Johnson plays the early stretch as an office comedy, all interruption and improvised confidence, then lets the tone harden as the numbers grow, which describes how a business changes people better than any speech about ambition would. Two hours of meetings, demos and deadlines, with more suspense in them than most thrillers manage. The affection in the early scenes is what gives the rest of it weight.

The insect powder is meant for work, but the household has found a better use for it. Bill Lee exterminates bugs; he and his wife would sooner take the poison than sell it, and their friends are Beat poets who keep talking while the two of them go under. Then the apartment gives way to a Mediterranean city that will not hold still, where a drug is cooked out of a centipede, a doctor named Benway turns up offering help nobody asked for, and the typewriter has opinions and a mouth. David Cronenberg shoots it at room temperature, deadpan and bureaucratically patient with the grotesque, which is what makes it funny and what makes it hard to sit through, often in the same shot. Writing is the real subject: work done without the writer's knowledge, on machines that are alive and not on his side.

Carlos Marighella wrote poems and held office before deciding that neither would answer the government that seized power in 1964. Wagner Moura puts 155 minutes of action-cinema grammar behind that decision, weapons and safe houses and pursuit, then spends the room it buys on the household left behind, a wife and a son who are not a subplot but the running cost. The dictatorship is filmed as an apparatus rather than a villain: orders, offices, men with jobs, a state racist by design. Casting a Black revolutionary as the man who drives a genre picture is itself the position being taken. The genre is not a sweetener; it is the claim that this history belongs in the form people actually watch, in a country whose coup the CIA backed.

A mother leaves for the United States with her boyfriend and does not take her daughter. What Lilya keeps is an apartment, a town the Soviet Union used to organise and no longer does, and a set of adult problems arriving years early: money, food, the neighbours' verdict, the men who notice a teenager with nobody standing behind her. Lukas Moodysson holds the camera at her height and lets the situation do its own explaining, so when a man named Andrei arrives with the offer of work in Sweden, it reads exactly as it would to a girl who has not heard a true sentence in months. The hardness of this film is not a style. It is the arithmetic of who has power over whom, worked through patiently.
